comment.value: This paper introduces a large-scale dataset, OrthoLoC, along with a method-agnostic technique named AdHoP that significantly improves localization accuracy. It offers a more effective utilization of orthographic geodata compared to previous works. The paper received uniformly positive evaluations from four reviewers, all recommending "Accept". Based on a comprehensive consideration of the manuscript, the reviewer comments, and the authors' rebuttal, the area chairs have decided to accept the paper.

We thank all the reviewers for their constructive discussion. Below are our work's merits and rebuttal results summarized.

**Brief summary of our contributions**

- We proposed a framework that can 6DoF localize and calibrate UAVs using only freely available government geodata (DOPs/DSMs).

- Our dataset represents a first-of-its-kind high-precision dataset at scale containing UAV imagery from over 47 locations with different views and altitudes that are aligned with geodata as well as other modalities such as depth maps and 3D meshes. We have >4k orthoimages with domain shift.

- We introduced a method-agnostic AdHoP technique that achieves significant improvements in localization and calibration accuracy for various matching algorithms.

**Brief summary of rebuttal stage**

We are glad reviewers appreciated our “systematic exploration” with a “thoroughly designed evaluation framework” (3dPu), describing it as “very meaningful” (2SQS) and “comprehensive” with “convincing” novelty (ffbv). They noted “higher accuracy ground truth poses than other datasets” (ffbv) and a “reasonably large number of frames in realistic scenarios” (CCKH). AdHoP was recognized for “substantially improving localization accuracy” (3dPu, ffbv) while being matcher-agnostic (2SQS). The paper was found “clear and easy to follow” with “quality figures” (2SQS, ffbv).

Concerns were raised regarding paradigm clarification, technicalities, and data accessibility. We addressed these as follows:

- We clarified how using government geodata (high quality with regular updates) as reference data enables new research directions and how our dataset contributed to this research with its unique features.

- We provided explanations regarding technical aspects such as validating accuracy, details about the dataset pipeline workflow for reproducibility, and the temporal validity of the geodata.

- We distinguished our work from previous studies, positioned AdHoP with learning-based homography estimators as future research, and committed to expanding related work with image-retrieval methods.

- We also promised to include .tiff formats along with C++ documentation.

We are grateful that our responses addressed reviewers’ concerns. 3dPu raised their score to “accept”; all reviewers submitted acknowledgments. CCKH noted geographic limitations were “not critical” for publication. All promised improvements from the discussions will be incorporated in the final version.

Respectfully,

Authors

Thank you for your follow-up. For this dataset, we used our in-house workflow as described in B.4.1 (Georeferenced 3D Scene Reconstruction). We manually ran a collection of SfM pipelines from the provided list and selected the best output for each scene individually. The decision was based on quantitative evaluations of bundle-adjustment reprojection errors and GCP and/or RTK errors, as well as on qualitative assessments by projecting keypoints, as was done for the benchmarked localization methods presented in the paper.
Based on our experience, regardless of the software (also open-source ones), starting with default settings already provides good results if the images are high-quality (no motion-blur, high resolution) and sufficiently overlapped. Greater accuracy can be achieved by tuning parameters; for instance, by changing feature detectors in SfM pipelines (e.g., SIFT vs. ORB) or adjusting depth-map resolution in MVS software for complex scenes.

Thank you for your response. We are happy that some of our answers clarified some of your concerns. We would like to add a few details regarding the remaining ones:

A1: We see historical orthoimages as a super-category of governmental orthoimages. Generally, historical orthoimages can be outdated, and since they may come from different providers, they might also be unreliable, obtained by outdated technology, and lack associated 3D data. 
In contrast, by restricting the selection to those coming from governmental agencies, we ensure access to regularly updated data (e.g., OpenGeoData.NRW provides yearly updates), which serve decision-making processes (e.g., urban planning). They provide orthoimages of high quality, enabling accurate and precise methods. We rely on governmental data to ensure that recent orthoimages and surface models are included.

A3: We see the reviewer's point and agree that domain reference orthoimages might seem limited compared to other data sources. As noted by the reviewer, one reason behind this is the lack of an open geoportal in the US. As mentioned in the previous point, this is also a consequence of relying solely on high-quality governmental data instead of using disparate historical orthoimages. Our hope is that our work will foster stakeholders' interest, motivating more agencies to acquire and open such data to the research community.

We thank the reviewer for the thorough and constructive feedback. We appreciate the time taken to examine our work in detail and provide valuable suggestions. Please find our responses below.

**Q1: "The dataset seems to be more incremental than paradigm shifting. Using orthoimage for visual navigation is not a novel idea"**

**A1:** We thank the reviewer for this important observation and for pointing out the relevant reference [1]. We believe our work makes a significant contribution to the field, beyond a simple incremental step, especially with regard to available datasets.

Notice that the standard paradigm in the field is localization through precise sensors [2,3], pre-built 3D models [4,5], or specialized databases of posed images [6,7,8]–all costly solutions which limit their applicability. Moreover, many existing approaches provide only partial pose estimation (e.g., 3DoF in [9] or missing yaw/altitude in [2]). Our proposal to use governmental data for full 6DoF pose estimation and even for calibration represents a fundamental shift. The cited work [1] addresses a different problem (achieving accurate georeferencing of UAV-generated orthoimages using historical orthoimages), while we tackle the inverse: 6DoF localization/calibration of UAV images using existing governmental orthoimages (DOPs) and surface models (DSMs).

Here we highlight our key contributions:

* **First large-scale 6DoF dataset using governmental geodata**: Our dataset enables benchmarking and training of **6DoF localization and calibration** methods using **only governmental DOPs and DSMs**, eliminating the need for costly preprocessing or specialized infrastructure (see Table 1 and Sections 3.4, B.3).

* **Cross-domain coverage**: Among datasets that utilize external sources to increase the domain gap of orthoimages and provide 3D reference data, we outperform existing datasets by incorporating **>4k orthoimages from external governmental sources** (vs. AnyVisLoc: 25, ALTO: 0: the domain shift in the provided DOPs in ALTO is minimal).
 
* **Alignment accuracy**: We achieve **~5cm median error** through GCP validation (alignment with governmental geodata). We demonstrate in Section B.3 that existing datasets (UAVD4L, CrossLoc, and the concurrent work AnyVisLoc) suffer from significant misalignments (either through projecting 3D points from geodata onto UAV images or via overlaying the reconstruction DOP and the DOP from external sources) (Appendix Figure 4).

* **Outperforming other UAV datasets with geodata**: Datasets providing geodata are limited to UAV-VisLoc, AnyVisLoc, SUES-200, and ALTO. Only AnyVisLoc and ALTO provide 3D reference data. AnyVisLoc is a concurrent dataset focusing on 3DoF localization and presents misalignment of its reference data (see Figure 4-c in Appendix). ALTO has UAV images with nadir perspective only (less challenging), high altitude (not compatible with low-flying drones), and no domain shift between UAV images and reference data. In contrast, our dataset provides **oblique and nadir** perspectives, **low and high** altitudes, **aligned DOPs and DSMs paired** with UAV images, and **precise 6DoF poses**. Crucially, with **47 locations** across diverse geographic settings using **47 different cameras**, we far exceed existing datasets providing 3D reference data (AirLoc: 1, UAVD4L: 2, AnyVisLoc: 25, ALTO: 1, VPAIR: 1).

* **Privacy-preserving design**: We uniquely decouple UAV images from their georeferencing, addressing **geographic privacy concerns** often ignored in existing datasets (Section B.4.2).

We believe our dataset will encourage researchers to develop UAV localization methods that work directly with governmental geodata. Our benchmarks show that this task is far from being solved: existing state-of-the-art matchers fail when applied to this cross-domain challenge of matching UAV imagery with governmental geodata. Our dataset provides the opportunity to push this unexplored domain further, particularly as such data becomes increasingly accessible in the EU and as real-world applications would benefit from on-the-fly localization without preprocessing requirements.

**Q2: "An evaluation of the accuracy of the model is lacking" & "Details about GCP are missing"**

**A2:** Thank you for highlighting these important aspects and for suggesting the relevant reference on mapping quality prediction [10].

Our GCPs were carefully selected following established best practices similar to those validated in [10]. We manually chose GCPs at precise features such as road marking edges, ensuring optimal visibility and spatial distribution across the mapping area. The 3D positions were obtained from either vehicle-based Mobile Laser Scanning point clouds or high-precision governmental geodata, providing 2D-3D correspondences that are introduced into the bundle adjustment optimization during SfM reconstruction (Section B.4.1, Georeferenced 3D scene reconstruction). Though [10] proposes an advanced predictive framework for optimizing GCP placement in complex environments, our empirical results demonstrate that careful manual selection based on established practices achieves the high accuracy levels required for downstream tasks.

We evaluate dataset accuracy through multiple validation approaches. First, we verify UAV pose accuracy via SIFT keypoint projection from orthoimages onto UAV images using DSM-lifted 3D positions (Section B.3, Appendix Figure 4). Second, we validate the reconstructed 3D model alignment through GCP error analysis, achieving a median Euclidean distance error of ~5cm (Section 3.4). This accuracy level demonstrates proper alignment with governmental geodata, which can be visually verified through the interactive visualizer on our project page where the reconstructed orthoimages overlay precisely with official geodata layers.

We will add a dedicated paragraph in the revision in Section B.4.1 detailing GCP selection criteria with visual examples, annotation protocol, and error distribution analysis.

**Q3: "Out of domain reference orthoimages are limited"**

**A3:** We respectfully argue that our cross-domain data introduces more realistic challenges than temporal variations alone. Governmental orthophotos are captured using different sensors, orthorectification methods, and color balancing pipelines compared to our drone imagery. Years-apart acquisitions also introduce major structural and appearance changes that same-period flights cannot replicate (Appendix Fig. 2). This domain shift is critical, as real-world applications must handle geodata from various global providers with temporal gaps–2-3 years in urban areas, 5+ years in rural, as in our dataset.

We agree that expanding geographic diversity would strengthen the dataset and will consider this for future extensions. Nonetheless, we provide over 4k samples with DOP shifts and 806 with both DOP/DSM shifts–more cross-domain coverage than any existing dataset. The largest performance drop occurs with DOP shifts alone, highlighting current limitations in matching algorithms; DSM shifts further degrade performance. We believe our dataset offers valuable benchmarks for reducing domain gaps.

**Q4: "Dataset format"**

**A4:** We chose .npz format for its self-contained nature–each sample packages all data (UAV images, DOPs, DSMs, camera parameters, 3D point maps, 3D meshes, etc) in a single file, preventing missing file errors and ensuring consistency.

We have documented the format in our README (Getting Started > Structure of the Dataset section):
* **Intrinsics:** Full 3×3 intrinsic matrix
* **Extrinsics:** 3×4 world-to-camera pose matrix (first 3 columns = rotation, 4th column = translation)

We fully understand the importance of C++ compatibility in robotics. We will provide a TIFF version of the dataset alongside information about cross-language libraries (e.g., cnpy) for .npz access. We thank the reviewer for pointing this out, as it will help us make the dataset more accessible to the broader robotics community.

**References**

[1] TSAI, Chung-Hsien; LIN, Yu-Ching. An accelerated image matching technique for UAV orthoimage registration. ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing.

[2] KINNARI, Jouko; VERDOJA, Francesco; KYRKI, Ville. GNSS-denied geolocalization of UAVs by visual matching of onboard camera images with orthophotos. In: 2021 20th international conference on advanced robotics (ICAR).

[3] DAI, Xi, et al. Navigation of simultaneous localization and mapping by fusing RGB-D camera and IMU on UAV. In: 2019 CAA Symposium on Fault Detection, Supervision and Safety for Technical Processes (SAFEPROCESS).

[4] YAN, Shen, et al. Render-and-compare: Cross-view 6-dof localization from noisy prior. In: 2023 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo (ICME).

[5] ZHU, Juelin, et al. LoD-Loc: Aerial Visual Localization using LoD 3D Map with Neural Wireframe Alignment. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2024, 37. Jg., S.

[6] CHEN, Shuxiao, et al. Real-time geo-localization using satellite imagery and topography for unmanned aerial vehicles. In: 2021 IEEE/RSJ international conference on intelligent robots and systems (IROS).

[7] WU, Rouwan, et al. Uavd4l: A large-scale dataset for uav 6-dof localization. International Conference on 3D Vision (3DV), 2024.

[8] YAN, Qi, et al. Crossloc: Scalable aerial localization assisted by multimodal synthetic data. In: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

[9] KINNARI, Jouko, et al. LSVL: Large-scale season-invariant visual localization for UAVs. Robotics and Autonomous Systems, 2023.

[10] CLEDAT, Emmanuel, et al. Mapping quality prediction for RTK/PPK-equipped micro-drones operating in complex natural environment. ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, 2020.

We thank the reviewer for the careful and thoughtful comments and we appreciate pointing out the typos, which we will correct in the revised paper. Please find our responses to each point below.

**Q1: Missing reference - "A Visual Localization Benchmark for UAVs in Complex Multi-Terrain Environments" [1]**

**A1:** We have carefully reviewed Chen et al.'s work [1] and recognize its valuable contributions to UAV localization. You are absolutely right that this work should be discussed in our paper. In our paper, we focused on 2DoF to 6DoF localization methods in the literature review and omitted image retrieval-based approaches as our focus involves localization with higher degrees of freedom. However, while their approach differs from ours - they use image retrieval from a geolocated database while we directly leverage governmental geodata - both methods address the fundamental challenge of UAV localization. For completeness and to provide a better overview of existing approaches to UAV geolocalization, we will add references for image retrieval-based localization methods as part of the related work in our revised manuscript.

**Q2: Details about SfM/MVS software**

**A2:** Thank you for highlighting this gap in our methodology description. For our reconstructions, we used standard drone photogrammetry software for SfM/MVS reconstruction. Specifically, commercial solutions such as DJI Terra, Pixpro, Pix4Dmapper, RealityCapture, and Agisoft PhotoScan, as well as open-source alternatives like Meshroom, COLMAP with OpenMVS, MicMac, and WebODM can achieve similar results. All these tools follow similar photogrammetric principles and produce comparable quality reconstructions when provided with sufficient image overlap, highly accurate RTK positions, and GCPs. The exact choice depends on availability, budget, and specific project requirements. We will add these software options in Section B.4.1 to ensure reproducibility.

[1] Chen, J., Wen, G., Jian, H., & Fan, X. (2025). A Visual Localization Benchmark for UAVs in Complex Multi-Terrain Environments. IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing.

We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments. Your suggestion about deep learning-based homography estimation methods provides a great opportunity to clarify our approach. The idea of incorporating deep learning homography methods (IHN, RHWF) is indeed interesting and could potentially enhance performance.

For this work, we deliberately chose to showcase AdHoP using the most straightforward pipeline - normalized DLT+RANSAC - as a first step in demonstrating the dataset's utility. Although simple, this approach offers several advantages:

* Interpretability of the geometric errors and transformations: we can pinpoint exactly why a localization fails (e.g., too few feature matches, poor correspondence distribution, or geometric degeneracies) rather than dealing with opaque neural network predictions

* Generality across different scenarios without domain-specific assumptions

* No training requirements or ad-hoc domain focus choices

While learning-based homography estimation is certainly promising, it would introduce significant complexity, including hyperparameter tuning, training data selection, domain generalization validation, and feature extraction choices.

We will add this suggestion to the future work of our manuscript.

We thank the reviewer for the thorough and constructive comments. Please find our responses to specific queries below.

**Q1: "distinction from existing UAV datasets"**

**A1:** We appreciate the opportunity to clarify our dataset's unique contributions. Our dataset is specifically designed for 6DoF localization and calibration using geodata (DOP and DSM) as reference data, which fundamentally distinguishes it from existing datasets and represents a paradigm shift from costly traditional approaches.

As shown in Table 1, existing datasets are designed for localization methods that rely on other reference data types (posed image databases, meshes, point clouds, or LoD models). We move from this paradigm to a new one leveraging existing geodata (specifically DOPs and DSMs) as the only reference to enable 6DoF UAV localization and calibration. Notably, we provide:

* The **first large-scale** dataset with UAV images **paired** with **DOPs and DSMs** enabling direct **6DoF localization** and **calibration**

* **>4k orthoimages from external governmental sources** - far exceeding AnyVisLoc (25) and ALTO (0: minimal domain shift exists in the provided DOPs in ALTO), enabling domain shift performance evaluation and helping to close the domain gap in neural networks

* **Accurate alignment** and **high pose accuracy** (~5cm median GCP error) - Our evaluation exposed significant misalignments in existing datasets: UAVD4L and CrossLoc show projection errors between geodata and UAV images, while AnyVisLoc provides only 3DoF poses with misaligned references (see Appendix Figure 4). Our aligned DOP+DSM pairs ensure accurate 6DoF poses.

* Current UAV datasets with orthoimages and 3D reference data have critical limitations: AnyVisLoc offers only 3DoF poses with misaligned DSM data, while ALTO provides nadir-only views without domain shift. Our dataset uniquely features **aligned governmental DOP+DSM pairs** with accurate **6DoF** poses, **oblique and nadir perspectives** at **multiple altitudes**, and **47 locations** with **different cameras**.

* **Privacy-preserving design** through georeferencing decoupling (Section B.4.2) - a consideration ignored by most UAV datasets

This opens previously unexplored research directions for on-the-fly localization without preprocessing requirements. We will emphasize these distinctions in the final revision.

**Q2: "computing resources and timing metrics"**

**A2:** Thank you for highlighting this practical consideration. We kindly refer to Tables 2 and Appendix Table 3 (last columns) for measures about timing, with hardware specifications detailed in Section C.1. Our experiments show that localization speeds range from real-time to several seconds per image, depending on the matcher choice. While AdHop approximately doubles processing time, it reduces the error of more than half (up to 95%), showing its convenience in terms of costs/benefits.

In summary, we see room for flexibility: real-time applications can run with fast matchers without AdHop, while offline ones that prioritize precision can run more time-consuming pipelines.

**Q3: "temporal validity of the open geodata" and "potential compensation strategies for outdated information"**

**A3:** We greatly appreciate this insightful comment about temporal validity—a critical real-world challenge we aimed to address. Our dataset specifically captures temporal mismatches ranging from 2-8 years between geodata and UAV acquisitions, reflecting realistic update cycles (urban areas: 2-3 years, rural: 5+ years).

As shown in Table 4 (Appendix), all methods experience performance degradation under these temporal shifts, validating the reviewer's concern. Our dataset enables researchers to develop two concrete compensation strategies: (1) benchmarking matcher robustness to temporal changes—our results indicate dense matching methods show greater resilience by exploiting more correspondences from unchanged regions, and (2) fine-tuning algorithms using our temporally-mismatched pairs to improve generalization.

Thanks to our accurate ground-truth poses despite temporal shifts, we believe that our dataset provides a valuable tool to investigate such a challenge. We will incorporate this discussion in our manuscript.

summary.value:
They introduce a new dataset for benchmarking image-based UAV localization and camera calibration methods.  The dataset consists of several modalities: imagery, digital orthophotos, digital surface models, 3D point maps, and 3D meshes.  They include in total 16.4K images.  

They use the dataset to compare many different SOTA image matching algorithms in terms of pose accuracy/recall and speed.  They also evaluate camera calibration but find that this is a difficult task for UAV imagery.

They also evaluate a two-step process called AdHoP where they first estimate a homography and then re-compute matches using the warped view.

strengths_contributions.value:
They provide a comprehensive comparison table which convincingly highlights the novelty and advantages of their dataset.  By using structure-from-motion and GPS/RTK or GCP alignment, they achieve higher accuracy ground truth poses than other datasets.  Other advantages of their dataset are the wealth of modalities, the geographic diversity, and the examples of domain shift where the illumination or scene structure changes between the reference and query views.

The proposed AdHoP method is straightforward, but they show it leads to a significant improvement in performance for most of the matching methods in an ablation study.

They provide experimental evidence as well as a thorough theoretical justification for why self-calibration is difficult for UAV imagery.
The paper is nicely written with quality figures.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
I found one missing reference:

Chen, J., Wen, G., Jian, H., & Fan, X. (2025). A Visual Localization Benchmark for UAVs in Complex Multi-Terrain Environments. IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing.

They didn’t provide much detail about what SFM/MVS software was used; this could be helpful to future researchers aiming to build similar datasets.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value:
The dataset contains thousands of aerial images of the built environment and includes images of people's homes and backyards, etc.  However the images were taken at high elevation and are not so high resolution that identifying information is retained.  The authors acknowledged these issues and took steps to address them.

Another issue is that the dataset only covers regions in the USA and Germany and so is not truly geographically diverse.

dataset_code_comments.value: The code and data are all publicly accessible and well documented.

additional_feedback.value:
L25 "image retrieval poses" sounds strange but I understand what you are referring to.  "which is inaccurate" -> "which are inaccurate"
L170 "visually verify" -> "visually verifying"

final_justification.value: The authors addressed my concerns and provided useful new information in their responses.  I maintain my positive evaluation of the paper.

summary.value: The authors propose a multimodal (2D and 3D) dataset for visual navigation in UAV. The dataset contains views from UAV flight with both NADIR and oblique facing views, orthoimages and digital surface models reconstructed from the aerial view using photogrametry and corresponding orthoimages from public geoportals (for domain shift). State of the art algorithms are evaluated on the proposed dataset.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The idea is sound, the proposed data is fitting for the proposed task. 

- The dataset has a reasonably large number of frames, acquired in realistic scenarios. 

- The authors took good care of anonymizing the the data by removing absolute georeferencing information.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The dataset seems to be more incremental than paradigm shifting. Using orthoimage for visual navigation is not a novel idea [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924271617302277], and looking at Table 1, the differences with existing datasets do not seem groundbreaking.

- An evaluation of the accuracy of the model is lacking. Accuracy of the dataset is an important parameter, which should be evaluated in the paper (e.g. using the method proposed here [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924271620301428] ), as high accuracy would increase the value of the dataset. More details on the GCP used should be provided.

- Out of domain reference orthoimages are limited to a single country out of 2. As this is one of the main benefits of the proposed dataset, I feel it limit the potential impact of the proposed dataset, as only 806 samples have both the across domain DOP and DSM, far less than the claimed 16k samples. I understand that this is probably due to the absence of open geoportal in the US compared to germany, but a workaround would have been to just do a different flight on a different day. Different weather conditions and cars on the street would already have been much closer to a real life scenario.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value:
The main page for the dataset is available at: https://deepscenario.github.io/OrthoLoC/

From there, direct links allow to access the data repository and code repository are provided.

This is a detail, but it really bother me that the json format used to store intrinsic and extrinsic parameters have unclear labels. Is this json format used by a specific tool? I would much rather have a field for the focal length, one for the principal point with an u and v field. Same for extrinsic. The The x, y, z coordinate should be labelled as such. The orientation should be labelled as orientation (is it a quaternion? if yes, the w, x, y, z components should be labeled) If the pose is a matrix why is it 4x3 and not 3x4? These are small details that can make the life of the people using the dataset complicated. If the json are not clear, at least the ReadMe in https://deepscenario.github.io/OrthoLoC/ should make the storage format explicit.

Also, part of the data is given in numpy npy format. tiff would be preferable for people using something else than python. In robotics and navigation, c++ is still common use.

additional_feedback.value: Overall I feel that the paper is technically sound, propose an interesting idea but is weak in term of impact. I am not sure it pass the bar for Neurips (I am sure it can be accepted in a dedicated venue later on in case it gets rejected). nevertheless, I am willing to give it a 4: borderline accept, without enthusiasm. I am waiting for the later authors-reviewer discussion to see if I upgrade or downgrade my review.

final_justification.value: The authors have addressed my comments in their rebuttal and during the discussion phase. I have checked the comments and discussion of other reviewers and all seems to agree that the paper can be accepted. As such, I have increased my score to a 5 accept from a 4 borderline accept.

title.value: OrthoLoC: UAV 6-DoF Localization and Calibration Using Orthographic Geodata

TLDR.value: We present OrthoLoC, a large-scale UAV localization dataset pairing aerial imagery with orthographic geodata, enabling a new localization paradigm. Our AdHoP technique enhances matching-based localization pipelines.

abstract.value: Accurate visual localization from aerial views is a fundamental problem with applications in mapping, large-area inspection, and search-and-rescue operations. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources (e.g., no internet connection or GNSS/GPS support), making large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical. Surprisingly, little attention has been given to leveraging orthographic geodata as an alternative paradigm, which is lightweight and increasingly available through free releases by governmental authorities (e.g., the European Union). To fill this gap, we propose OrthoLoC, the first large-scale dataset comprising 16,425 UAV images from Germany and the United States with multiple modalities. The dataset addresses domain shifts between UAV imagery and geospatial data. Its paired structure enables fair benchmarking of existing solutions by decoupling image retrieval from feature matching, allowing isolated evaluation of localization and calibration performance. Through comprehensive evaluation, we examine the impact of domain shifts, data resolutions, and covisibility on localization accuracy. Finally, we introduce a refinement technique called AdHoP, which can be integrated with any feature matcher, improving matching by up to 95% and reducing translation error by up to 63%. The dataset and code are available at: https://deepscenario.github.io/OrthoLoC .
